{"lessons": ["

Essere and avere: the two pillars

Just like \"to be\" and \"to have\" in English, these two verbs are irregular and show up everywhere. Learn them by heart, out loud.

essere (to be)avere (to have)
iosonoho
tuseihai
lui, leièha
noisiamoabbiamo
voisieteavete
lorosonohanno

The subject is often left out: the verb ending is enough. Most of the time you just say Sono francese; \"Io sono francese\" is for emphasis or contrast (io… e tu?).

Sono francese e ho trent'anni.I'm French and I'm thirty (literally: I have thirty years).

Unlike English, age is expressed with avere (Ho trent'anni, \"I have thirty years\"), and so is hunger: avere fame (to be hungry, literally \"to have hunger\"). A profession takes no article: Sono medico, \"I'm a doctor\" — no word for \"a\". A yes/no question is made with intonation alone, with no word-order change: Sei di Parigi?

The trap: the h is never pronounced; it's only there to tell words apart in writing. ho (I have) / o (or), ha (he has) / a (to, at), hanno (they have) / anno (year). In the same way, è with an accent means \"he/she/it is\", while e without an accent means \"and\": Luca è italiano e Anna è spagnola.

", "

Masculine, feminine, plural

In Italian, almost every noun ends in a vowel, and that vowel often shows the gender. For the plural, you change the last vowel: you don't add an -s.

SingularPluralExample
-o (masculine)-iil fratello → i fratelli
-a (feminine)-ela sorella → le sorelle
-e (masculine or feminine)-ilo studente → gli studenti, la chiave → le chiavi

Nationalities follow the same rule: italiano, italiana, italiani, italiane; francese, francesi (same form for masculine and feminine). Unlike English, they're written with a lowercase letter.

Two traps: l'amico → gli amici (\"ch\" sound as in \"church\"), but l'amica → le amiche (the h keeps the hard \"k\" sound). And gli occhiali is always plural, like \"glasses\" in English.

", "

Articles

English gets by with \"the\" and \"a\". Italian has many more, because the article changes with gender and number, and also with the first letter of the word that follows.

Before…Definite singularDefinite pluralIndefinite
masculine, consonantil libroi libriun libro
masculine, s + consonant or zlo zaino, lo studentegli zaini, gli studentiuno zaino
masculine, vowell'amicogli amiciun amico
feminine, consonantla borsale borseuna borsa
feminine, vowell'amicale amicheun'amica
Ho uno zaino e una borsa.I have a backpack and a handbag.

Remember lo / gli / uno before s + consonant and before z: lo zaino, lo studente, lo stadio. And the apostrophe: un amico (masculine, never an apostrophe), but un'amica (feminine).

title: Essere and avere
topic: essere and avere in the present; definite and indefinite articles; gender and plural of nouns
why: First lesson of the unit "Introducing yourself": essere, avere and the articles are laid down slowly, before any other verb. The learner mixes up è and e ("il treno e a orario") and gets lo wrong ("alle stadio"): both points are practiced from the start.
